opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that a model's failures are rarely just about the model. They're about the relationship between the model, the data it was trained on, and the world it's actually deployed into. Only the domain expert really understands that third piece.

Aggregate metrics like mean average precision or accuracy on a held-out set are useful, but they compress everything into a single number. They tell you that something is going wrong, not why or where. When you start digging, the failures cluster. Maybe the detector struggles with pedestrians at dusk, or with a particular camera's lens distortion, or with a class that's visually ambiguous because the annotation guidelines were inconsistent. Automated tools can help surface those clusters, through embeddings, uncertainty estimates, or similarity search. But deciding whether a cluster is a real failure mode, a labeling problem, or an acceptable edge case requires judgment that comes from knowing the domain.

Take a radiologist, an agronomist looking at crop imagery, or an engineer who has spent years with a manufacturing line. They look at a set of misclassified images and immediately say, "Oh, those are all from the night shift, the lighting rig is different," or "That's not actually a defect, it's a known artifact of the sensor." That kind of insight just isn't in the pixels or the labels. It's tacit knowledge.

There's also a prioritization question. Not every failure matters equally. A domain expert knows which mistakes are costly and which are tolerable, and that should drive where you invest in more data, relabeling, or architectural changes.

So I see it as a loop. The tooling should make it fast and easy for experts to explore the data and the model's behavior together, visually and interactively, and then their insights feed back into data curation and retraining. In my experience, the teams that do this well aren't the ones with the fanciest architectures. They're the ones who've built a tight feedback loop between the humans who understand the problem and the models trying to solve it. Data-centric work is human-centric work, really.

r002.rationale: It mentions embeddings, uncertainty estimates, and similarity search, but does not describe using model logits to group outputs for human visual inspection.

r003.rationale: It states that deciding whether a cluster is a true failure mode, labeling issue, or acceptable edge case requires judgment from domain knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the short version is that a model can tell you it's wrong, but it can't tell you why it's wrong, and the "why" is where all the value is.

Think about what a typical evaluation gives you. You get an aggregate number, maybe a confusion matrix, maybe some per-class metrics. That's a symptom. It tells you the pedestrian detector drops ten points on some slice, but it doesn't tell you that the slice is "pedestrians partially occluded by parked cars at dusk, captured from the left-side camera." Nobody labeled that slice. It's not in your metadata. It's a concept that only exists once a person looks at a few hundred failures and goes, "oh, these all have something in common."

That act of pattern-finding across failures is a genuinely human skill, at least today. The expert brings two things the model doesn't have. One is domain context. If you're building a model for a warehouse robot or a surgical camera, the person who knows the environment knows which failures are benign and which are catastrophic, and knows what the long tail actually looks like in practice. The second is the ability to form a hypothesis. Automated tools can cluster embeddings and surface outliers, and we use them, but clustering gives you groups, not explanations. A human looks at the cluster and names it, and naming it is what lets you act on it. Now you can go collect more of that data, or write a targeted test, or change the labeling instructions.

There's also a data quality piece that people underestimate. A huge fraction of what looks like model failure is actually label failure, or a mismatch between what the annotation guidelines said and what the annotators did. The model learned exactly what you told it, and what you told it was inconsistent. You only discover that by having someone who understands the task actually look at the images alongside the predictions and the ground truth.

So my view is that the tooling should be built around amplifying that person, not replacing them. Get the right failures in front of the expert fast, let them slice and query and visualize, and let the machine do the tedious part. But the diagnosis, the moment of "I know what's going on here," that's still a human judgment, and I think it will be for a while.

r001.rationale: The response describes an expert examining failures for patterns and recognizing that a group of failures has something in common, which communicates looking for common structure across failures.

r002.rationale: It mentions clustering embeddings and surfacing outliers, but does not describe grouping outputs using model logits for human visual inspection.

r003.rationale: It says the expert supplies domain context, names failure clusters, and makes the diagnosis through human judgment.

astra-6.text:
Because the model can tell you what it predicted, but it can’t necessarily tell you why that prediction is wrong in a way that’s meaningful for the application. A metric might tell us that performance has dropped, but it doesn’t tell us whether we have a labeling problem, whether the data represents the conditions we care about, or whether the model has learned some incidental cue instead of the concept we intended.

The human expert brings that context. They can look at failures and recognize, “These are all cases where the object is partly occluded,” or, “This distinction actually matters in our domain, even though the labels don’t capture it.” That turns a collection of errors into a hypothesis you can test. So the expert is essential to connecting model behavior to the task—and deciding what to change next.

r002.rationale: It does not mention logits, clustering outputs, or inspecting clusters visually.

r003.rationale: It says a human expert brings domain context to recognize failure patterns and explain why they matter to the task.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a model can tell you what it predicted, but it can’t necessarily tell you why that prediction is wrong in a way that’s meaningful for the application. You might look at an aggregate accuracy number and see that performance has dropped, but that doesn’t tell you whether the problem is lighting, occlusion, a gap in the training data, or even an ambiguity in how the task was defined.

The human expert brings context. They can look at a set of failures and say, “These are actually the same kind of mistake,” even when the images look quite different at the pixel level. And they can distinguish an error that’s relatively harmless from one that makes the system unusable.

So I see diagnosis as an interaction. We want computational tools to help surface patterns and organize examples, and we need the expert to interpret those patterns and decide what we should change. That’s what turns a collection of incorrect predictions into a useful next step.

r002.rationale: It mentions computational tools surfacing patterns and organizing examples, but does not describe using model logits to cluster outputs for human visual inspection.

r003.rationale: It explains that experts use context to interpret failure patterns and determine what they mean for the application, conveying that diagnosis requires human judgment.
